messages.subject: Models hang on 'running chain 1...'
messages.body_plain:

messages.subject: Re: Models hang on 'running chain 1...'
messages.body_plain:
Oliver, I'm surprised to hear that it can hang for that long.  There are a number of small things that happen inside runMCMC(), after the message "running chain 1" and before the MCMC begins sampling (and hence the progress bar appears).  The only one of those which I think could take significant time is a call to model$calculate(), which calculates all the log-densities for every node in the model (top-level parameters, latent states, and also the data likelihood), which is somewhat precautionary, but sometimes necessary to ensure the model is fully initialized before the MCMC actually begins.  If your model is large, this call to model$calculate() can take a while, but in that case the MCMC would also generally take a lot of time.  So I'm a little surprised.  If you're interested to share your model code, I can take a closer look.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Models hang on 'running chain 1...'
messages.body_plain:
Olivier, thanks for bringing this to my attention.  This is a bit of an over-sight on my part.

There were some recent changes in NIMBLE's MCMC system, w.r.t. how it handles thinning vs. burnin.  (Specifically, which happens first?  Are burnin samples discarded from *post-thinning* samples, or are burnin samples discarded first, and the remaining samples thinned?  To completely resolve this question, any entry point to NIMBLE's MCMC now discards burnin samples *first*, then the remaining samples are thinned, e.g. (10000 - 2000) / 10 = 800 posterior samples returned; see help(runMCMC), Details section).

A result of this change, as an implementation detail, is that burnin samples specified through runMCMC() do *not* trigger the MCMC progress bar to begin, and instead the progress bar begins once the *post burnin* samples are being collected (and simultaneously thinned).

That is what you're experiencing, the fact that the 1000 burnin samples do not trigger the progress bar, which only begins starting at sample # 1001.  In combination with the pre-processing that takes place (e.g., model$calculate(), and a few other things), it gives the behaviour you're seeing, which I successfully recreated.

The upshot is that everything is working correctly, only the progress bar is misleading.

Let me give a think about the best way to restructure the implementation to address this, which I agree is unsatisfying.

I'll be in touch.

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: "Warning: slice sampler reached..."
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jose,

It's hard to say.  This is a trap we added in the last release to try to catch conditions when the slice sampler is in a bad state, which could conceivably lead to an infinite loop.  This could occur if there is a bad initial condition, or something is invalid (NaN or Inf) in the model, or there is a bimodal conditional distribution.  Is it happening early in the MCMC or late, once or many times?  Is it a univariate slice sampler or part of the AF_slice sampler?  If it is univariate, you could try replacing it with a RW (random walk Metropolis-Hastings).  Most of the core team is in one state of travel or another, but you could send us more about the example (on-list or off-list) if you're still stuck and we'll look at it but perhaps not right away.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Jacobian adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jeremy,

Thanks for the question.

I might need some clarification on what you want to achieve.  NIMBLE will use the parameters however you have declared them.  If the three parameters follow a distribution, and then function(s) of the three parameters are used elsewhere in the model, NIMBLE will treat them as following the distribution as declared.  But if what you want is that the distribution should really be defined on the transformed parameters, one way to do that would be to write a user-defined distribution (for the vector of three parameters) and use that in the model.  That user-defined distribution could include a Jacobian adjustment or whatever other math defines the prior that you want.  Writing user-defined distributions is covered in the User Manual.  If I've misunderstood your need here, can you state it more explicitly?

It would also be possible to write a custom sampler that in effect changes the distribution from what is given in the model.  You could copy and modify NIMBLE's samplers to do so, but I think it would be easier to write a custom distribution, so that any sampler will work correctly.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Jose for sharing a reproducible example off-list.  For the benefit of other list readers, here is a simplified summary of what happened.

There was a case like:

for(i in 1:N) {
   a[i] ~ dpois(lambda)
   b[i] ~ dbin(p, a[i])
}

where a[i] are random effects and b[i] are data.

The initial values for a[i] did not ensure that every a[i] >= b[i].  As a result, some of the binomial log probabilities could start at -Inf, and the slice sampler for a corresponding a[i] couldn't get started.

We'll have to give some thought to handling such a case (any suggestions?).  In the meantime, please be aware that sometimes alarming behavior from nimble is simply the result of incomplete or problematic initial values.

Thanks again to Jose for the helpful example.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Jacobian adjustment
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Jeremy.

I interpret what you are saying as wanting a custom distribution for the triplet (mu, sigma, xi) that you have derived from independent distributions for (q1, q2, q3) along with the function relating the two triplets.

Here are two ways you could implement that in NIMBLE, both using user-defined distributions.

Method 1:  Define (mu, sigma, xi) as a vector of three parameters, say theta[1:3].  Use

theta[1:3] ~ dMyCustomDistribution(parameters of the distributions of q1, q2, q3)

Then in dMyCustomDistribution, you can write the full pdf of theta[1:3], which will include pieces from the distributions of (q1, q2, q3) as well as the Jacobian, as you have derived.  In this method, the distributions for (q1, q2, q3) would not appear in the model code.  They would simply appear in dMyCustomDistribution.

Method 2: You could define a dummy data node, whose value need not even matter, in order to build an additional log density term into the graph.  That term would be the Jacobian need you.  This would look like the following

q1 ~ dgamma( ... )
q2 ~ dgamma( ...)
q3 ~ dgamma( ...)
dummy ~ dMyJacobian(q1, q2, q3, parameters of q1, q2, q3)

Now there will be a node "dummy" in the graph, with parent nodes q1, q2, q3 as well as their parameters.  If you write dMyJacobian (again, following our User Manual on how to write your own distribution) to return the log Jacobian term you need, it will be added into the likelihood.  For example, let's say you have a "RW" (adaptive random-walk Metropolis-Hastings) sampler on a parameter "alpha" of q1.  The stochastic dependencies of alpha will include q1 and dummy.  That means that the sum of log probabilities used in the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance ratio will include a term from dgamma for q1 and a term for dummy that provides the Jacobian.  When you write dMyJacobian, its first argument will be a deviate "x", which will be passed as "dummy", but you need not use it in the calculation.  Other samplers or algorithms should work too, because the graph defined by these declarations include the pieces you need.

Let me know if that gives you enough to move forward or if that was too rough an explanation.

-Perry

Hi Itzik,

Thanks for the question.

I don't completely follow your question, but let me try to explain what nimble should be be doing.  The observations are passed as data, but the (unknown) states are simulated by the particle filter.  For example, in the first example in section 8.1.1, in the nimbleModel call, y is given as data, but not x.  In the call to buildBoostrapFilter, the unknown states are indicated to be in variable "x".  This means that the "x[i]" will be simulated.

Even though a model declaration says "x[i] ~ dnorm(x[i-1] * a + b, 1)", the "rnorm" function will be used if this node is simulated by an algorithm.  The declaration means "x[i] follows this distribution", and then whichever function (dnorm or rnorm) is needed will be used (depending on whether the algorithm code has "calculate" or "simulate", respectively).

In your model, if the states are "x", then the particle filter will determine how to simulate from x[t-1] to x[t] using the graphical model declared by your code.  It looks like c[t] depends on x[t-1], and x[t] depends on c[t] and x[t-1].  The algorithm will use these in correct (topologically sorted) order, in this case c[t] before x[t].

One way to check that the steps are being called as you expect would be to run the particle filter uncompiled and use R's debugging to see when functions are called.  You can include "browser()" statements in the w nimbleFunction (which presumably you wrote), and you could do "debug(rnorm)" to catch rnorm being called.

Hope this helps.  Let us know further questions.  Often we can be more helpful if you include a full reproducible example.

Dear developers & users.

I am trying to construct a simple particle filter for discrete states and observations. Specifically, for each time t, there are 3 arrows on a computer screen, with each arrow pointing either right or left. Then, a target appears on one side of the screen. One of the cues predicts the target with some high probability (e.g 75%), and the others point at random. The cues change roles from time to time, such that a previous cue becomes random and a new one becomes predictive of the target.
In terms of the state-space model, this means that there are 3 possible discrete states, such that the probability of the state to continue to the next trial is defined as tau, and is a free parameter
The probability that the target will appear at the direction to which the relevant cue has pointed is gamma, which is also a free parameter.

Here is the model. The model is given the cues (a matrix of 3*T, with 1 indicating a right-pointing cue and -1 a left pointing cue), the targets (with 1 indicating a right target, and 0 a left target)
stateSpaceCode<-nimbleCode({
  gamma~dunif(0.51,0.99)
  tau~dunif(0.0001,0.9999)

  x[1]~dcat(lambda[1,1:3])
  lambda[1,1]<-1/3
  lambda[1,2]<-1/3
  lambda[1,3]<-1/3

  prob[1]<-equals(cues[1,x[1]],1)*gamma+equals(cues[1,x[1]],-1)*(1-gamma)

  target[1]~dbern(prob[1])

  for (t in 2:nTrials){
    x[t]~dcat(lambda[t,1:3])
    lambda[t,1]<-equals(x[t-1],1)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],1))*(1-tau)/2
    lambda[t,2]<-equals(x[t-1],2)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],2))*(1-tau)/2
    lambda[t,3]<-equals(x[t-1],3)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],3))*(1-tau)/2

    prob[t]<-equals(cues[t,x[t]],1)*gamma+equals(cues[t,x[t]],-1)*(1-gamma)
    target[t]~dbern(prob[t])

  }
})

The issue I'm having is related to the definition of the auxiliary variable 'prob'. The idea is that prob should be separate for each particle of x. That is, it should define the probability of the target appearing to the right, as a function of the relevant arrow (according to a specific particle x) pointing right (1) or left(-1) and gamma.
However, first, when building the model I get this warning:

running calculate on model (any error reports that follow may simply reflect missing values in model variables) ... Error in if (x1 == x2) 1 else 0 : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Second, when examining 'prob' I get the same value (0.75 or 0.25) for each column of the particles matrix  (i.e. for each time point). That is - it seems to ignore the value of x for the relevant particle, and just choose a constant value for all.

Any help would be appreciated.
Thanks,
Isaac.

relCue=rep(NA,nTrials)

genCues[1,other]<-sample(c(-1,1),1)
genCues[1,genCues[1,]==0]<-1

for (t in 2:nTrials){

  relCue[t]=relCue[t-1]
  if (max(t==changeT)==1) {
    #    opt<-opt[opt!=relCue[t-1]]
    if (length(opt)>1) {relCue[t]=sample(opt,size = 1)} else {relCue[t]=opt}
  }
  valid=runif(1,0,1)
  if (valid<=validity){genCues[t,relCue[t]]<-genTarget[t]} else {genCues[t,relCue[t]]<--1*genTarget[t]}
  #other=c(1,2,3)
  #other<-other[other!=relCue[t]]
  genCues[t,-relCue[t]]<-sign(runif(2,-10000,10000))
  #  genCues[t,genCues[t,]==0]<-1

}

test=data.frame(genCues,genTarget,relCue)

stateSpaceCode<-nimbleCode({
  gamma<-0.75
  tau<-0.9

  x[1]~dcat(lambda[1,1:3])
  lambda[1,1]<-1/3
  lambda[1,2]<-1/3
  lambda[1,3]<-1/3

  prob[1]<-equals(cues[1,x[1]],1)*gamma+equals(cues[1,x[1]],-1)*(1-gamma)

  target[1]~dbern(prob[1])

  for (t in 2:nTrials){
    x[t]~dcat(lambda[t,1:3])
    lambda[t,1]<-equals(x[t-1],1)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],1))*(1-tau)/2
    lambda[t,2]<-equals(x[t-1],2)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],2))*(1-tau)/2
    lambda[t,3]<-equals(x[t-1],3)*tau+(1-equals(x[t-1],3))*(1-tau)/2

    prob[t]<-equals(cues[t,x[t]],1)*gamma+equals(cues[t,x[t]],-1)*(1-gamma)
    target[t]~dbern(prob[t])

  }
})

  gamma=0.75,
  tau=0.9
)

bootstrapFilter<-buildBootstrapFilter(stateSpaceModel,nodes='prob',control=list(saveAll=T))
compiledList<-compileNimble(stateSpaceModel,bootstrapFilter)
compiledList$bootstrapFilter$run(1000)

post<-as.matrix(compiledList$bootstrapFilter$mvEWSamples)

Thanks a lot!

Thanks for the complete example.  That makes it much easier to look at.

Regarding the incomplete initialization: stateSpaceModel$initializeInfo() reveals that x, lambda and prob are not fully initialized when the model is created.  As the message says, this is not an error, but it is letting you know.

I think the incomplete initialization is responsible for the message later, when the particle filter runs, about indices out of bounds.  So in your case, full initialization will be needed.

For you to get running, I recommend either fully initializing up to at least the first state or using the blanket approach of:
stateSpaceModel$simulate()
stateSpaceModel$calculate()

For us, I will file an issue to see if the particle filters could take a more careful initialization approach automatically in a case like this.

Regarding the unchanging values of 0.75 or 0.25 for each prob[t] throughout the particle filter run: I think you are not specifying the nodes argument as needed.  This should be a variable that contains a sequence of stochastic nodes representing the system state.  In your model I think this would be 'x'.  When I use nodes = 'x', then I do see heterogeneity in the particle sample of x values.  I believe it needs to be a stochastic node in order for the setup code to correctly determine the right sets of nodes to be simulated and/or calculated as the particle filter proceeds.

Let us know further issues.

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: Ragged arrays
messages.body_plain:
Hi Arthur,

A common way to do it would be:

  for (i in 1:I) {
    for (j in 1:J[i]) {

      y[i, j] ~ dnorm(mu[i], 1)

    }
    mu[i] ~ dnorm(m, var=s2)
  }

y will become a matrix variable with sizes I x max(J[]), but it will be effectively ragged because only the declared nodes with be in the model (the directed acyclic graph, if you like to think of it that way).  The data can be provided as a full matrix.  Values of elements that don't exist in the model shouldn't matter.

Unfortunately in the current release, there is an over-zealous error trap that incorrectly traps some ragged arrays and gives an error message when none is needed.  A work-around to disable this problem is nimbleOptions(allowDynamicIndexing = FALSE), as long as you do not need stochastic indices in the model.

This should be fixed in a release soon.

-Perry

Given you're using the bootstrap filter, I wanted to make you aware

that incorrectly omitted the previous weights when calculating the new
weights after any step in which the particles were not resampled.

to the new version to get the corrected version of the bootstrap
filter for your work. Let us know if you have questions about this.

Chris

On Mon, Jul 16, 2018 at 1:41 AM, Perry de Valpine
<pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Itzik,
>
> Thanks for the question.
>
> I don't completely follow your question, but let me try to explain what
> nimble should be be doing.  The observations are passed as data, but the
> (unknown) states are simulated by the particle filter.  For example, in the
> first example in section 8.1.1, in the nimbleModel call, y is given as data,
> but not x.  In the call to buildBoostrapFilter, the unknown states are
> indicated to be in variable "x".  This means that the "x[i]" will be
> simulated.
>
> Even though a model declaration says "x[i] ~ dnorm(x[i-1] * a + b, 1)", the
> "rnorm" function will be used if this node is simulated by an algorithm.
> The declaration means "x[i] follows this distribution", and then whichever
> function (dnorm or rnorm) is needed will be used (depending on whether the
> algorithm code has "calculate" or "simulate", respectively).
>
> In your model, if the states are "x", then the particle filter will
> determine how to simulate from x[t-1] to x[t] using the graphical model
> declared by your code.  It looks like c[t] depends on x[t-1], and x[t]
> depends on c[t] and x[t-1].  The algorithm will use these in correct
> (topologically sorted) order, in this case c[t] before x[t].
>
> One way to check that the steps are being called as you expect would be to
> run the particle filter uncompiled and use R's debugging to see when
> functions are called.  You can include "browser()" statements in the w
> nimbleFunction (which presumably you wrote), and you could do "debug(rnorm)"
> to catch rnorm being called.
>
> Hope this helps.  Let us know further questions.  Often we can be more
> helpful if you include a full reproducible example.
>
> -Perry

messages.subject: NIMBLE version 0.6-12 released
messages.body_plain:
We’ve released the newest version of NIMBLE on CRAN and on our website.

Version 0.6-12 is primarily a maintenance release with various bug fixes.

Changes include:

- a fix for the bootstrap particle filter to correctly calculate
weights when particles are not resampled (the filter had been omitting
the previous weights when calculating the new weights);
- addition of an option to print MCMC samplers of a particular type;
- avoiding an overly-aggressive check for ragged arrays when building
models; and
- avoiding assigning a sampler to non-conjugacy inverse-Wishart nodes
(thereby matching our handling of Wishart nodes).

Please see the NEWS file in the installed package for more details.

- Chris Paciorek for the NIMBLE Development Team
